blocks.content: A container is a running instance of an image: the image's read-only layers, plus one writable layer just for this instance, plus an actual running process, isolated from everything else on the host.
1. Three Things Combine to Make a Container
blocks.text: 1. Three Things Combine to Make a Container

blocks.content: An image alone is just files sitting on disk, inert. A container exists the moment Docker adds a writable layer on top of that image and starts a process inside it. Take away any one of those three pieces (the image's layers, the writable layer, or the running process) and you no longer have a container.

blocks.alt: Image layers, a writable layer, and a running process together

blocks.content: 2. A Container Can Exist Without Running
blocks.text: 2. A Container Can Exist Without Running

blocks.content: "Container" does not only mean "currently running." A container can be running, paused (frozen in place, still consuming its allocated memory), or stopped (process exited, but the container and its writable layer still exist on disk until explicitly removed).

blocks.alt: A container can move between running, paused, and stopped

blocks.content: 3. Isolation, Recapped from the Container's Side
blocks.text: 3. Isolation, Recapped from the Container's Side

blocks.content: From inside, a container sees its own process list, its own network interface, and its own filesystem, none of it shared visibly with the host or other containers, even though underneath they are all using the same kernel (the namespaces and cgroups mechanics behind this are covered fully in the Docker Internals module).

blocks.alt: Its own process, network, and filesystem view

blocks.content: 4. Reads from the Image, Writes to Its Own Layer
blocks.text: 4. Reads from the Image, Writes to Its Own Layer

blocks.content: A container reads files from the image's read-only layers freely, but any file it creates or modifies goes into its own private writable layer instead, never touching the shared image underneath. This is exactly why many containers can run from one image at once without interfering with each other.

blocks.alt: Reads flow from the image, writes stay local to the container

blocks.content:
docker run -d --name web nginx
docker run -d --name web2 nginx
# Two independent containers, same image, each with its
# own writable layer, running side by side.

code.content:

docker run -d --name web2 nginx
# Two independent containers, same image, each with its

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container is an image's layers, plus a writable layer unique to that instance, plus a running, isolated process.
A container still exists (on disk, addressable) even while stopped, it is only gone once explicitly removed.
